title: REST principles (resources, nouns in URLs, statelessness)
hook: Representational State Transfer (REST) is not a framework — it is a set of constraints for designing networked APIs around resources (nouns), standard HTTP methods (verbs), and stateless servers that return representations like JSON.

blocks.text: REST, defined by Roy Fielding, treats every URL as a resource identifier — customers, orders, invoices — not as remote procedure names. The server does not store client session state between requests; each call carries whatever context it needs (tokens, ETags, idempotency keys). Representations (JSON, XML, PDF) are negotiated via headers. Hypermedia (links in responses) is the ideal but most teams ship JSON with stable URLs and OpenAPI contracts instead.

entries.plainDefinition: An architectural style using resources, representations, and uniform HTTP interfaces instead of RPC-style action URLs.
A noun identified by a URL. Collections use plural paths; individual items add an id segment.
The server does not remember prior requests. Authentication and context ride on every call.
The bytes returned for a resource — usually JSON with the same fields the client sent on create/update.

blocks.text: RESTful naming makes APIs predictable: clients guess /orders/{id}/items without reading docs. Stateless servers scale horizontally — any pod can handle any request if auth is self-contained. Violating REST (verbs in URLs, 200 for everything) creates brittle clients, broken caches, and interview red flags.

blocks.title: REST is not CRUD only
blocks.body: Create, read, update, delete map to POST, GET, PUT/PATCH, DELETE — but REST also cares about cacheability, layered systems, and uniform interfaces. A 'REST-ish' JSON API is fine for internal services; public APIs need stricter status codes and versioning.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Pick the HTTP method
items.body: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partial update, DELETE removes.

items.title: Return the right status
items.body: 201 + Location on create, 204 on delete with no body, 404 when the resource id does not exist.

items.title: Keep server stateless
items.body: Store session in JWT or server-side token store keyed by Authorization header — not in-memory per connection.

snippet.label: RESTful minimal API routes
snippet.explanation: Plural collection path, id segment for items, correct status codes. MapGroup keeps routes DRY — similar to Express Router mounted at /api/orders.

snippet.label: Controller with resource naming
snippet.explanation: [controller] token resolves to 'Invoices' — plural controller name becomes /api/Invoices. CreatedAtAction sets Location header pointing to the new resource.

snippet.label: Anti-pattern — RPC verbs in URL
snippet.explanation: Cancellation is a state change on the order resource, not a new verb endpoint. Email lookup is a filtered collection read — use query parameters on the collection URL.

blocks.title: REST routing in ASP.NET Core vs Express
Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using POST for every operation including reads. Singular URLs (/order) mixed with plural (/orders) in the same API. Returning 200 with { success: false } instead of 4xx. Storing shopping cart state only in server memory without a token — breaks scale-out.

blocks.text: REST vs RPC vs GraphQL is a tradeoff interview. REST wins for cacheable public resources and CDN-friendly GETs. gRPC wins for internal high-throughput binary contracts. GraphQL wins when clients need flexible field selection — at the cost of cache complexity. In production, measure p95 latency and error budgets per resource — not ideological purity. HATEOAS (hypermedia links) is rare in JSON APIs but _links in Problem Details and pagination next/prev URLs are practical subsets.

blocks.title: API style tradeoffs
rows: Harder HTTP caching, N+1 resolver risk

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Defining REST as 'using JSON and HTTP' without mentioning resources, statelessness, or uniform interface. Insisting every API must be hypermedia-driven HATEOAS when your team ships OpenAPI + JSON. Not knowing when POST /search is acceptable (complex query bodies) vs GET with query strings.

interviewTakeaways: REST centers on resources (nouns), representations (JSON), and stateless servers — not RPC action names in URLs.
Plural collection paths, nested sub-resources, and honest HTTP status codes make APIs predictable and cache-friendly.
Statelessness means auth and context on every request — design for horizontal scale, not sticky sessions.

60s: URLs name resources. HTTP methods express intent. Server stores no client session between calls. Return 201 with Location on create, 404 when id missing. Avoid /cancelOrder — PATCH the resource or POST to a sub-resource.
Follow-up: when would you choose gRPC or GraphQL over REST for the same domain?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'REST means CRUD' gets you rejected — uniform interface and cacheability matter too.
Mixing /order and /orders in one API confuses clients and breaks route conventions.
Strong answer: 'Nouns in URLs, verbs in HTTP methods, stateless handlers, correct status codes. RPC-style URLs are for exceptions like OAuth token endpoints, not domain CRUD.'
introducedIn: Roy Fielding dissertation (2000); ASP.NET Core Web API since 1.0

jsTsCorrelations.note: express.Router() at '/api/orders' mirrors MapGroup in minimal APIs. Both encourage nesting sub-routes for sub-resources without verb-heavy paths.
NestJS @Controller('orders') + @Get(':id') maps closely to ASP.NET Core attribute routing. Both use class-based controllers; minimal APIs are closer to Express route callbacks.
